item.title: US government builds $30bn stock portfolio across 43 deals in chips, minerals and quantum
item.description:
For investors, a government stake has become a recurring catalyst in chips, critical minerals and quantum computing. Announcements have tended to support the share prices of the companies involved, and they add a policy premium to those sectors. The Intel swing shows the flip side: government holdings are as exposed to market volatility as any investor’s. The concentration in Intel also leaves the portfolio’s headline gains sensitive to a single stock. The untested legal footing of some deal structures is a risk worth watching, since any legal challenge could unsettle the companies involved. The Venezuelan oil stake is a small but notable link between the portfolio and energy policy.

Washington now runs a stock portfolio worth tens of billions without anyone formally in charge of it, and like any investor, it is learning that Intel shares can go down as well as up.

Summary:

  • The US government has announced 43 deals involving equity stakes or warrants since the start of Trump’s second term, totalling around $30 billion
  • Intel is the largest holding: around $9 billion invested, peaking at $61 billion in value before falling to roughly $41 billion
  • There are 14 chip deals, at least 16 in metals and minerals, and nine stakes in quantum computing firms
  • Notable deals include around $2.2 billion for Korea Zinc and a $1 billion commitment to IBM’s quantum chip facility
  • Analysts say some bespoke deal structures rest on untested legal authority, and free-market advocates have criticised government overreach

The Trump administration has built up equity stakes in more than 40 companies since the start of the president’s second term, assembling a government stock portfolio spanning chipmakers, miners and quantum computing firms at an unprecedented pace, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

The US government has announced 43 deals involving stock ownership or warrants that can later be converted into equity, with total spending of around $30 billion, according to the Council on Foreign Relations. Largely thanks to a rally in Intel shares, the portfolio is sitting on gains of tens of billions of dollars.

Semiconductors account for 14 of the deals, and Intel is by far the largest. The government invested around $9 billion for a 9.9% stake in August 2025. A months-long rally lifted the value of that holding to as much as $61 billion, though a sharp selloff in recent weeks has cut it to roughly $41 billion. Other chip-related deals include a $150 million investment in laser maker xLight, finalised in June, and around $390 million in equity funding for four companies announced by the Commerce Department last week.

Metals, critical minerals and natural resources make up at least 16 deals, eight of which include loans. Among the largest is a Defense Department investment of around $2.2 billion, alongside private investors, in Korea Zinc, driven by US and South Korean concerns that China could restrict access to key materials.

The government has also announced stakes in nine quantum computing companies, though most deals have yet to close. The largest is a $1 billion commitment to IBM, which plans to spend a further $1 billion of its own to build the country’s first quantum chip-making facility. The portfolio also includes a 35% stake in a company seeking access to Venezuelan oil.

Many of the deals come with loans or supply agreements and use bespoke structures that, according to analysts, rest on untested legal authority. The more hands-on approach has drawn criticism from free-market advocates concerned about government overreach, while supporters see it as a way to strengthen industries central to US strategic competition. A Council on Foreign Relations fellow said the holdings should be managed like any portfolio, but noted that Washington has many dealmakers and no chief investment officer.

As the portfolio grows, how it is governed, and whether returns are judged in strategic or financial terms, is likely to become a bigger question for investors in the companies involved. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Alphabet slides over 9% after hours as search miss and $9bn cash burn overshadow Cloud
item.description:
The market is rewarding AI spending that generates cash and punishing spending that consumes it, judging by Microsoft’s after-hours gain against Alphabet’s slide. For the AI supply chain, Alphabet’s guidance for significantly higher 2027 capex adds to Samsung’s call that chip shortages will deepen, supporting chip and data centre names even as it weighs on Alphabet itself. The search miss is the more lasting concern, as it gives the first concrete evidence for the long-feared risk that AI answers erode Google’s core ad revenue. Expect pressure on wider megacap tech sentiment at the open, with attention turning to Amazon’s results.

-

Google Cloud is booming, but investors just learned that AI may be eating search and that the bill for the build-out is now coming out of the cash pile.

Summary:

  • Alphabet shares fell more than 9% after hours
  • Free cash flow was negative by around $9 billion against breakeven expectations, the second straight quarter of cash burn
  • Revenue of around $127.6 billion and ad revenue of around $82 billion both missed, and adjusted EPS of $2.67 missed $3.02
  • Google blamed slower search ad growth on greater use of AI Mode and will roll out AI Mode ads internationally
  • The CFO said 2027 capex will rise significantly from the 2026 range of $195 billion to $205 billion, and flagged margin and cash flow pressure
  • Cloud revenue more than doubled to around $30.7 billion, with a backlog of around $560 billion

Alphabet shares fell more than 9% in after-hours trading after the Google parent reported a miss in its core search advertising business and a sharp deepening in cash burn, as heavy spending on AI infrastructure overshadowed another blockbuster quarter for Google Cloud.

The company reported negative free cash flow of around $9 billion in the third quarter, against analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. It was Alphabet’s second straight quarter of negative free cash flow, following a burn of around $6 billion in the previous quarter, the first time in 22 years as a public company that the figure had turned negative.

Revenue of around $127.6 billion fell short of the roughly $128.2 billion consensus. Advertising revenue of around $82 billion missed expectations of about $83.4 billion, more than offsetting a beat in Cloud. Adjusted earnings per share of $2.67 also missed the $3.02 analysts had expected, and net income available to shareholders fell 25% to around $26 billion.

Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said search advertising growth slowed more than expected because of greater use of AI Mode, the chatbot-style search interface in which Google is still testing ads. He said Google would begin rolling out ads in AI Mode in international markets. Investors have been watching closely for signs that AI-generated answers could erode traditional search revenue, and one portfolio manager said the stock was likely to stay under pressure until search shows AI is adding to growth rather than taking from it.

Spending concerns added to the pressure. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said capital expenditure would rise significantly in 2027 from this year’s forecast range of $195 billion to $205 billion, though she did not give a figure. She also flagged near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity, and warned that building up inventory of Google’s tensor processing units would weigh further on free cash flow.

Cloud remained the bright spot. Revenue more than doubled to around $30.7 billion, ahead of estimates, and Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, appearing on the earnings call for the first time, said sales of Google’s TPU chips had become a meaningful contributor. Ashkenazi said the Cloud backlog had grown to around $560 billion, with more than 55% expected to be recognised as revenue within 24 months.

The contrast with Microsoft was stark. Its shares rose more than 5% after the bell, helped by free cash flow that beat estimates. For Alphabet, the next test is the size of its 2027 spending plan, and whether search growth stabilises as ads are rolled out more widely in AI Mode. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Samsung Q3 operating profit jumps ninefold to record 107 trillion won on AI chip boom
item.description:
Samsung’s guidance that the chip shortage will deepen next year is the most market-relevant line. It points to continued pricing power for memory makers and supports the read-through from SK Hynix’s upbeat outlook a day earlier. That backdrop fits with the heavy capex plans from US hyperscalers, Microsoft’s call among them, which underpin demand. The net profit miss may temper the reaction, though the operating figures were pre-announced and the market will focus on the outlook. The weakness in mobile and display highlights how concentrated Samsung’s earnings have become on a single cycle, leaving the stock exposed to any wobble in AI spending sentiment.

---

Yesterday:

  • SK Hynix Q3 operating profit beats at 83tn won, unveils 100tn won shareholder payout plan

--- Samsung has become an AI memory company with a phone business attached, and for now that’s a very profitable thing to be.

Summary:

  • Q3 operating profit rose nearly ninefold to around 107 trillion won (about $80 billion), in line with Samsung’s estimate
  • Revenue of around 195 trillion won was in line, but net profit of around 75 trillion won missed estimates of about 84 trillion won
  • The chip division earned 106.5 trillion won, while mobile posted a loss of around 600 billion won and display earned around 1.1 trillion won
  • Samsung expects memory demand to keep expanding in Q4 and the chip shortage to deepen next year
  • Foundry revenue rose sharply and is expected to grow by a double-digit percentage in Q4
  • A third-quarter dividend of around 30 trillion won, or 4,601 won per share, was declared

Samsung Electronics posted a record operating profit for the third quarter, up nearly ninefold from a year earlier, as booming demand for chips used in artificial intelligence drove its semiconductor business to unprecedented earnings, Reuters reported.

Operating profit reached around 107 trillion won, roughly $80 billion, matching the company’s preliminary estimate and up from about 12 trillion won a year earlier. Revenue came in at around 195 trillion won, also in line with guidance. Samsung said it became the first global technology company to post quarterly operating profit above 100 trillion won.

Net profit was weaker relative to expectations, at around 75 trillion won against an LSEG SmartEstimate of roughly 84 trillion won, a shortfall of more than 8 trillion won.

The chip division generated an operating profit of 106.5 trillion won, accounting for almost all of the group’s earnings. Samsung said memory chip demand would keep expanding in the fourth quarter and that the chip supply shortage would deepen next year. Its foundry business, which makes chips to order for other companies, saw revenue rise sharply in the quarter and is expected to grow by a double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter.

The rest of the business painted a very different picture. The mobile division swung to an operating loss of around 600 billion won, while the display unit earned around 1.1 trillion won. Samsung expects demand weakness in its display business to continue into 2027.

The company also announced a third-quarter dividend totalling around 30 trillion won, or 4,601 won per share.

The results came a day after cross-town rival SK Hynix reported strong earnings and an upbeat outlook, which helped ease concerns that AI-driven chip profits could lose momentum and lifted shares of both companies. Investors nonetheless remain cautious about how long the current pace of AI spending can last.

With Samsung forecasting a tighter chip market next year, the key question for investors is whether hyperscaler demand holds up as major customers report spending plans of their own. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBNZ’s Breman says chances of a December rate hike are high after surprise hold at 2.75%
item.description:
Breman’s comments push back against the dovish reading of Wednesday’s hold and look aimed at steadying the New Zealand dollar, which she has said could add to imported inflation if it stays weak. Pricing of around 77% leaves room for further repricing toward a December hike if incoming data cooperates, which would support the currency and front-end yields. Her emphasis that timing is uncertain keeps the risk of a second hold alive, so the kiwi’s recovery may be gradual rather than sharp. Fuel prices remain the main external swing factor, linking the RBNZ path to oil and the Iran conflict.

-

A day after a hold that sank the kiwi, Breman is all but promising December, though she isn’t quite ready to put it in writing.

Summary:

  • RBNZ Governor Anna Breman told the New Zealand Herald that the chances of a December hike are high
  • She said all committee members agree further rate increases are likely, though timing depends on the outlook and inflation
  • The RBNZ held the cash rate at 2.75% on Wednesday, surprising markets, and the New Zealand dollar fell sharply
  • Markets now price around a 77% chance of a December hike
  • Breman said the bank will stay calm and focused on returning inflation to target

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman said on Thursday that the chances of an interest rate hike in December are high, sharpening her guidance a day after the central bank surprised markets by leaving the official cash rate unchanged at 2.75%.

In an interview with the New Zealand Herald, Breman said every member of the monetary policy committee agrees that further increases in the cash rate are likely, though the timing remains uncertain and will depend on the economic outlook and how inflation develops. Asked directly about the odds of a move in December, she said they were high.

The comments go further than the signal the RBNZ gave on Wednesday, when it held rates but said additional hikes were likely. That decision caught markets off guard. Before the announcement, pricing had pointed to a hike as close to a certainty, and the New Zealand dollar fell sharply after the bank held. Markets now price around a 77% chance of a hike in December.

The hold was itself a close call, with the committee split 4-3 and Breman among the majority who argued that two recent rate increases warranted time to assess their effects. At her press conference after the decision, she said tightening could need to extend into restrictive territory and flagged concern that a weaker currency could add to imported inflation at a time when fuel costs have risen further.

Fresh data has added weight to that concern. A business survey released on Thursday showed the share of New Zealand firms planning to raise prices climbed to its highest since May, with cost expectations remaining very high.

Breman also sought to reassure the public, saying that despite an uncertain environment, the RBNZ would remain calm and focused on its mandate of returning inflation to target.

The December decision will come alongside the Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts and a new projected path for the cash rate. Until then, inflation indicators, labour market data and the currency will be key in determining whether the high chance of a hike becomes a reality. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The view from China: CITIC Securities still sees a 25bp Fed hike in December
item.description:
CITIC’s call reinforces the market’s December hike pricing, but its view that the terminal rate stays near current levels points to a shallow end to the cycle rather than an extended run of increases. That combination supports the dollar into December, with less upside for Treasury yields further out. On oil, the brokerage sees no clear de-escalation path yet between the US and Iran, which argues for crude holding its risk premium. That in turn keeps upward pressure on the inflation backdrop the Fed is reacting to. Its note that dollar liquidity needs a fresh catalyst suggests funding conditions are unlikely to ease on their own in the near term.

---

Earlier:

  • Recap: Fed holds at 3.75%-4% in 10-2 vote as Cook dissents for a hike, December move in focus
  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 28 Oct: Fed holds rates, yield curve steepens as Big Tech earnings diverge

---

From China, CITIC Securities sees one more Fed hike and then a plateau, with oil, not the Fed, setting the pace for what comes after.

Summary:

  • CITIC Securities still expects the Fed to raise rates by 25 basis points in December
  • It sees the terminal rate in this cycle staying close to current levels
  • It said the October statement was more upbeat on growth but more guarded on policy guidance
  • It said officials’ post-meeting remarks were milder than in September, citing tighter credit and improving inflation expectations
  • It said Middle East developments do not yet offer a clear, lasting US-Iran de-escalation path, so oil may stay high
  • Further improvement in US dollar liquidity needs a fresh catalyst, according to the brokerage

Chinese brokerage CITIC Securities still expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December, but sees the peak for this tightening cycle staying close to current levels, offering a view from China that broadly aligns with US market expectations.

In its assessment of the Fed’s October meeting, CITIC said the decision to hold, which left the policy rate at 3.75% to 4%, was in line with expectations. It noted that the post-meeting statement sounded more positive on growth, while guidance on the path for policy was more guarded. According to the brokerage, remarks from Fed officials after the meeting were softer in tone than in September. They pointed to tighter credit conditions and inflation expectations moving in the right direction, and flagged changes to the policy meeting schedule over the next two years.

That schedule change, announced by Chair Warsh, will see the Fed vote on rates at seven of its eight meetings next year and six in 2028, with the remaining sessions devoted to strategy.

Despite the milder tone, CITIC sees a December hike as its base case. Its view that the terminal rate is unlikely to move much above current levels implies the brokerage sees limited room for tightening beyond that move. The meeting itself showed hawkish pressure on the committee, with two officials dissenting in favour of an immediate hike.

The brokerage also linked the Fed outlook to the Middle East. It said recent developments are not yet enough to put the US and Iran on a clear and lasting path toward de-escalation, and that oil prices could remain high until the situation becomes clearer. That matters for the Fed because elevated energy costs feed directly into the inflation picture policymakers are trying to bring under control.

CITIC added that any further improvement in US dollar liquidity would require a new catalyst. For markets, the brokerage’s message is that the December decision and the course of US-Iran diplomacy remain the two key variables shaping both rates and oil into year end. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6596 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZ business confidence rises to +53 as pricing intentions hit highest since May
item.description:
Firmer pricing intentions and inflation expectations stuck around 3.3% give the RBNZ little reason to ease off its tightening. The resilient activity readings also undercut any argument that the oil shock is crushing demand. For the New Zealand dollar, that is a modest support, though the currency’s weakness is itself feeding the services export boom. The oil link remains the main swing factor: ANZ’s data shows business sentiment tracking crude closely this year, so any renewed spike in prices tied to the Iran conflict would be the biggest threat to this resilience.

---

New Zealand business has taken the latest oil shock on the chin far better than it took the last one, but rising price plans mean the RBNZ will be watching just as closely as the bosses.

Summary:

  • ANZ business confidence rose 1 point to +53 in October, while expected own activity eased 2 points to +46
  • Reported past activity rose 4 points to +15, with all sectors positive
  • A net 52% of firms expect to raise prices, up 4 points and the highest since May, and the expected average increase rose to 1.9%
  • Cost expectations held at a net 82%, and inflation expectations were steady at 3.3%
  • Services export intentions hit a 25-year high, helped by the weak New Zealand dollar
  • ANZ said the second-quarter confidence shock has not been repeated despite the renewed rise in oil prices

New Zealand business confidence edged up in October and firms’ plans to raise prices climbed to their highest since May, the ANZ Business Outlook survey showed, suggesting the economy is weathering the renewed jump in oil prices better than many had feared.

Headline business confidence rose 1 point to +53, while expected own activity, which ANZ regards as the more reliable guide to the economy’s direction, eased 2 points to a still-solid +46. Reported past activity, which compares current trading with a year earlier, improved 4 points to +15, with every sector in positive territory.

Price pressures were mixed but leaned higher. A net 52% of firms expect to raise prices over the next three months, up 4 points, and the average expected price increase rose to 1.9%, the highest since June. Cost expectations held at a very high net 82%, while one-year-ahead inflation expectations were steady at 3.3%. ANZ noted that cost expectations have stayed contained despite higher fuel prices, but cautioned that firms are estimating increases from an already inflated starting point.

Among the other details, services firms’ export intentions jumped to their highest in 25 years, which ANZ linked to the weak New Zealand dollar, with tourism operators reporting strong forward bookings. Investment intentions slipped to +18 from +23, and employment intentions held at around +17. Wage expectations of around 2.8% suggest only marginal upside risk to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s wage forecasts, according to ANZ. Wellington recorded the highest regional confidence, while Canterbury was the lowest.

ANZ said the renewed rise in oil prices is a headwind for both New Zealand and the global economy, but that the survey matches what it is hearing from business owners: the confidence shock that brought activity close to a standstill in the second quarter has not been repeated. Some firms have been surprised by how well demand has held up despite price increases, while others are realising that continually putting off decisions such as investment carries its own risks.

With interest rates rising and pricing intentions firming, the next survey, due on November 30, will show whether that resilience can withstand both higher energy costs and tighter monetary policy. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil - The UAE’s second Hormuz bypass pipeline gets its firm timing; early 2027
item.description:
For oil, the report offers a medium-term offset to Hormuz risk rather than near-term relief, since no new bypass capacity arrives before early 2027. Until then, Gulf supply remains exposed to any renewed escalation, so the war-risk premium is unlikely to ease on this news alone. Once running, a second outlet to Fujairah would make more of the UAE’s medium sour crude secure for Asian buyers, which could narrow risk premiums on Gulf grades bought on term contracts. The bigger exposure remains with Gulf producers that lack comparable bypass routes, so a firm start date for Adnoc alone does not change the overall supply picture much.

Adnoc is building its way around Hormuz, but the new exit doesn’t open until early 2027, leaving the market to live with the strait for a while yet.

Summary:

  • Adnoc told some Asian refiners it may start supplying Upper Zakum crude from Fujairah in early 2027, Bloomberg reported
  • The crude would move via the new West-East 1 pipeline, bypassing the disrupted Strait of Hormuz
  • Adnoc said in May it was accelerating construction, and its CEO said the line was nearly 50% complete
  • The pipeline is expected to double Adnoc’s export capacity through Fujairah
  • The existing Habshan-Fujairah pipeline carries up to 1.8 million barrels a day
  • The UAE left OPEC with effect from May 1 and targets 5 million barrels a day of production capacity by 2027

Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. has told some Asian refiners that part of their crude supply from its offshore fields is likely to be delivered through a new pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz from early next year, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

According to the report, Adnoc has indicated it may begin supplying some Upper Zakum crude to term customers from the Fujairah terminal in the first months of 2027. Upper Zakum is produced from fields inside the Persian Gulf, meaning its exports would normally have to pass through Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted by the Iran war. The guidance is the most specific timeline yet for the project. Adnoc said in May that it was speeding up construction and that the pipeline would be ready next year, but gave no further detail.

The line, known as West-East 1, was fast-tracked in May. Adnoc Chief Executive Sultan Al Jaber said later that month that it was nearly half complete and that, once operational, it would double the company’s export capacity through Fujairah, which sits on the Gulf of Oman outside the strait. The UAE’s existing Habshan-Fujairah pipeline can already carry up to 1.8 million barrels a day.

The project is part of a broader effort by the UAE to protect its exports while Hormuz remains contested. The country, which left OPEC with effect from May 1, has been targeting crude production capacity of 5 million barrels a day by 2027.

The timeline matters for Asian buyers in particular, as they rely heavily on Gulf crude that must currently either transit the strait or compete for limited capacity on the existing bypass route. A second outlet would give Adnoc’s term customers a more reliable supply channel, although it would not remove the wider risk to the large volumes from other Gulf producers that have no comparable alternative.

Whether the start-up arrives on time, and how quickly flows ramp up, will be key for gauging how much Gulf supply can be insulated from any renewed escalation.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Peltz-led group offers $1.4bn to take Wendy’s private at $7.35 a share, a 20% premium
item.description:
Shares peaked at around $7.20, below the $7.35 offer, which suggests the market is pricing some risk that the deal won’t complete on these terms. The independent committee could push for a higher price, or the bid could falter, as Trian’s earlier take-private plans did. With net debt of around $2.4 billion against a $1.4 billion equity value, financing terms will be central to whether the deal holds together. For the wider restaurant sector, the bid highlights pressure on chains exposed to lower-income diners, and may stir speculation about other underperforming names becoming take-private targets.

---

After circling Wendy’s for nearly two decades, Peltz has finally put a price on it, betting a burger chain under pressure will mend faster out of public view.

Summary:

  • A Trian-led group offered $7.35 a share in cash for Wendy’s, valuing it at around $1.4 billion, a premium of roughly 20%
  • Wendy’s shares rose as much as about 17% to around $7.20
  • The consortium includes franchisee Flynn Group, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners
  • Wendy’s independent committee will evaluate the offer, with no assurance of a deal
  • Wendy’s withdrew its annual forecasts in August amid weak sales, and had net debt of around $2.4 billion in June
  • Trian considered a take-private in 2022 before backing away in 2023, and Wendy’s shares are down about 26% this year

An investor group led by billionaire Nelson Peltz has offered to take Wendy’s private in a deal valuing the burger chain at around $1.4 billion, arguing that the struggling business needs a turnaround best carried out away from public markets.

Peltz’s Trian Fund Management, which together with related parties holds a stake of around 16% in Wendy’s, is leading the group and has offered $7.35 a share in cash, according to a regulatory filing. The offer represents a premium of roughly 20% to Tuesday’s closing price, and Wendy’s shares jumped as much as about 17% to around $7.20 on Wednesday. The bid was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Trian is joined by Flynn Group, one of Wendy’s largest US franchisees with more than 340 restaurants, along with investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners. In a letter to the board, the group said private ownership would provide the patient, long-term capital needed to restore the business and its franchise system.

Wendy’s confirmed it had received the proposal and said an independent committee would review it, while cautioning that there was no certainty it would pursue the deal or any other strategic option.

The bidders described Wendy’s as being at a critical point, citing strained US consumers, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and fierce competition among burger chains. Sales have weakened as cost-conscious diners cut back, and the company withdrew its annual forecasts in August, when its chief executive acknowledged it was not performing to its potential. Peltz and Flynn said the business needs substantial investment to reduce debt and fund a turnaround. Wendy’s had net debt of around $2.4 billion as of late June. Analysts said a take-private made sense, given that a recovery is likely to be prolonged amid pressure on lower-income consumers and a soft burger market.

The offer caps a relationship of nearly two decades. Trian has long held board seats at Wendy’s, considered taking it private in 2022 before stepping back in 2023, and said in February that the shares were undervalued. With the stock down about 26% this year, the independent committee’s response is now the key next step. 

Harsh but mainly fair. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Hong Kong holds base rate at 4.25%: why the HKMA always moves in lockstep with the Fed
item.description:
For Hong Kong, the decision confirms that local borrowing costs stay tied to the Fed’s hiking path, regardless of domestic conditions. Mortgage holders and property developers are most exposed, because a December Fed hike would flow through to the base rate and from there to bank lending rates. The peg also means Hong Kong dollar assets carry US rate risk. Traders should watch Fed expectations, not the HKMA, when positioning for Hong Kong rate moves.

---

Earlier:

  • Recap: Fed holds at 3.75%-4% in 10-2 vote as Cook dissents for a hike, December move in focus
  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 28 Oct: Fed holds rates, yield curve steepens as Big Tech earnings diverge

---

Hong Kong’s rate decisions are made in Washington, and with a December Fed hike widely expected, the city’s borrowers are along for the ride.

Summary:

  • The HKMA held its base rate at 4.25%, as expected, after the Fed held at 3.75% to 4%
  • Hong Kong’s Linked Exchange Rate System, in place since 1983, keeps the currency between HK$7.75 and HK$7.85 per US dollar
  • The base rate is set at 50 basis points above the lower end of the Fed funds range, or a HIBOR-based average if that is higher
  • The HKMA defends the band by buying or selling Hong Kong dollars, which moves interbank rates
  • The peg means Hong Kong effectively imports US monetary policy
  • A December Fed hike would be expected to lift Hong Kong’s base rate in step

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority kept its base rate unchanged at 4.25% on Thursday, as expected, following the US Federal Reserve’s decision to hold its policy rate at 3.75% to 4%. The outcome was never in doubt, and understanding why explains how Hong Kong runs monetary policy.

Hong Kong has operated its Linked Exchange Rate System since 1983. Under it, the Hong Kong dollar is held within a narrow band of HK$7.75 to HK$7.85 against the US dollar. The HKMA commits to buy or sell Hong Kong dollars at either edge of that range, which keeps the currency anchored to the greenback. 

A fixed exchange rate comes with a trade-off: a city cannot run an independent interest rate policy while keeping its currency pegged. If Hong Kong rates drifted far from US rates, capital would flow toward whichever currency paid more, putting pressure on the peg. So Hong Kong effectively imports US monetary policy.

That link is written directly into the base rate formula. The rate is set at the higher of two measures: 50 basis points above the lower end of the Fed funds target range, or an average of short-term Hong Kong interbank rates, known as HIBOR. With the Fed’s range starting at 3.75%, adding 50 basis points produces exactly 4.25%. When the Fed moves, the HKMA follows.

Market forces back up the formula. If the Hong Kong dollar weakens to HK$7.85, the HKMA buys local currency, draining cash from the banking system and pushing interbank rates higher until the currency recovers. At the strong end, it sells Hong Kong dollars, adding liquidity and pushing rates down.

The practical consequence is that Hong Kong’s borrowing costs are set by conditions in the United States rather than at home. That matters now. The Fed held this week but signalled that inflation remains its priority, and markets widely expect a hike in December. If that happens, Hong Kong’s base rate is likely to rise in step, whatever the state of its own economy. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood struck an upbeat tone on the payoff from the company’s heavy spending on AI infrastructure, telling analysts on Wednesday’s earnings call that Microsoft expects to stay free cash flow positive this fiscal year even as capital expenditure climbs toward around $170 billion.

At LinkedIn, more than 10 million members use AI-powered job search each day and 25,000 customers use its agentic hiring tools. item.title: Gold heads for its biggest yearly drop in 11 years as the Iran war lifts yields and the dollar
item.description:
The poll shows the gold outlook is being driven by the Iran war’s knock-on effects rather than by safe-haven buying. Higher oil prices have fed through to yields, the dollar and expectations that rates will stay high, which raises the cost of holding bullion. That makes crude a key upstream driver for gold: any easing in oil and yields, for example on progress in US-Iran talks, would remove one of the main headwinds analysts cite. Silver carries extra downside risk because its industrial exposure leaves it vulnerable to softer solar demand on top of the rate pressure. The forecast gap between the two metals favours gold over silver.

---

---

The Iran war has turned gold’s usual crisis logic on its head, with oil-driven yields and a firm dollar doing the damage, but analysts are betting central banks will catch it on the way down.

Summary:

  • A Reuters poll of 30 analysts and traders put the median 2026 gold forecast at $4,495 an ounce, down from $4,509 three months ago
  • The 2027 gold forecast rose to around $4,650 from around $4,610
  • Gold has fallen from a January record near $5,600 to around $4,000, on course for its biggest yearly drop in 11 years
  • High yields, a strong dollar and higher-for-longer rate expectations, driven by the Iran war, are the main headwinds
  • Central bank purchases and physical demand from India and China are expected to provide support
  • Silver is forecast to average around $70 in 2026 and $67 in 2027, against a current price near $53, with weak solar demand weighing

Analysts have lowered their 2026 gold price forecast for a second consecutive quarter, citing high US Treasury yields, a strong dollar and expectations that interest rates will stay elevated for longer, though they still see prices recovering in 2027, according to a Reuters poll.

The survey of 30 analysts and traders, conducted over three weeks, produced a median forecast of $4,495 an ounce for 2026, trimmed from $4,509 in the previous poll three months ago. The 2027 median rose to around $4,650 from around $4,610.

The downgrade reflects a sharp reversal this year. Gold hit a record of around $5,600 an ounce in January but has since dropped to around $4,000. The Iran war pushed oil prices and Treasury yields higher and lifted the dollar, all of which reduced the appeal of bullion, an asset that pays no interest. Gold is now on course for its steepest annual decline in 11 years.

Even so, analysts see support building. Standard Chartered expects prices to consolidate and then recover over the coming months as investor attention turns to de-dollarisation and currency debasement. Respondents also pointed to strong central bank buying and solid physical demand. One analyst said that, barring an unexpected shock, steadier physical buying in India and China should underpin prices. The same analyst argued that continued central bank purchases send a signal about how official institutions are managing risk, which matters more than the volume of gold they buy.

The outlook for silver is weaker. Analysts expect it to average around $70 an ounce this year and around $67 in 2027, though that would still be above the current price near $53. Because silver is both a precious and an industrial metal, it is more exposed than gold to higher-for-longer rates. Respondents cited softer demand from the solar sector, substitution in manufacturing and cautious investor sentiment after this year’s wild swings, which included a record high of around $122 in January. With solar oversupplied and sentiment toward AI under pressure, silver is expected to underperform gold, and heavy ETF outflows this year have left the market in surplus.

The path for both metals now hinges largely on whether yields and the dollar ease from current levels.

item.title: Strategy's bitcoin buying hinges on one number: STRC at $100
item.description:
What is happening

Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, bought no bitcoin in the week of October 19 to 25. Instead it spent $204.9 million buying back its own STRC preferred shares, according to its October 26 filing with the SEC.

Those buybacks have helped lift STRC to about $99.36, its highest level in roughly five months and just shy of its $100 par value. Social media accounts have run with the next step: Michael Saylor is "set to resume heavy Bitcoin buying" once STRC gets back to $100.

That claim rests on a real, stated plan. Whether it plays out as "heavy" is a different question, and readers may get some answers soon. Strategy reports third-quarter results after the US close on Thursday, October 29, with a webinar at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

What STRC is and why $100 matters

STRC, nicknamed Stretch, is a perpetual preferred share with a variable dividend that Strategy pays monthly. The dividend is adjusted to keep the price anchored near its $100 par value, and Strategy raised the rate to 12% during the summer slump.

The $100 level matters because Strategy has said it will not sell new STRC below par. Above it, STRC becomes a fundraising tool again: Strategy can sell shares into the market and use the cash to buy bitcoin. It still has about $17.5 billion of STRC available to sell under its at-the-market (ATM) programme, and that figure has not moved in its weekly filings since at least June.

Management has been explicit about the link. Chief executive Phong Le told Bloomberg TV on July 14 that once STRC gets back to par, Strategy will issue more and buy bitcoin. So the condition in the social media post is accurate. It is just not new.

Bitcoin versus its own paper

The recent filings show where Strategy's cash has been going. Newest first:

Across those two weeks, Strategy spent about $18 on its own preferred shares for every $1 it spent on bitcoin. In the week in between, it bought 267 BTC for $22.1 million. It still holds 848,517 BTC at an average cost of about $75,446 per coin, so this is a change in the flow of new buying, not a retreat from the position.

For bitcoin traders, that flow matters. Strategy has been the market's most reliable corporate buyer, and a week without it removes a familiar source of demand. Bitcoin slipped below $80,000 on October 27, with analysts at TradingKey pointing to both spot ETF outflows and the Strategy pause, though a single week does not prove cause and effect.

Near par is not the same as par that holds

Here is the catch in the "heavy buying" headline. Much of STRC's recovery has come from Strategy buying the shares itself. Its latest buyback works out to an average of about $99.06 a share, right where the five-month high sits.

That support has a cost. After last week's buybacks, Strategy's USD Cash balance stood at $242.4 million, separate from a $4.83 billion USD Reserve set aside for preferred dividends and debt interest. The board lifted the preferred buyback authorisation from $2 billion to $3 billion on October 19, and about $957 million of it remains.

The real test comes at $100. To fund bitcoin, Strategy has to sell new STRC to outside investors. If demand at the current dividend is thinner than hoped, fresh issuance could push the price back below par and send Strategy back to buying its own paper. Saylor's informal goal of regaining par by September 8 has already come and gone, which suggests the last few dollars are the hardest.

What to watch next

  • Tonight's earnings call. Listen for any update on the STRC dividend rate, the buyback budget and the conditions for restarting STRC sales. A clear timetable would matter more than another round of "once we get to par".
  • STRC at $100 without help. The stronger signal is STRC holding at or above par in weeks when Strategy is not buying it back. Price support from the issuer itself proves little about outside demand.
  • Monday's filings. Strategy reports weekly. The line to check is STRC shares sold under the ATM. While that reads zero, the big funding channel is still shut, whatever the headlines say.
  • Bitcoin purchase size. Buying funded only by common stock sales has recently run at tens of millions of dollars a week. Heavy buying, by Strategy's own past standards, would be a much bigger number.

What would change the view: confirmed STRC issuance at par followed by sizeable bitcoin purchases in the same filing. Until then, treat the $100 level as a door that is nearly open, not one Strategy has walked through.

The practical takeaway for bitcoin traders: Strategy's weekly filing is one of the clearest demand signals in the market. It is worth reading alongside ETF flows, rather than relying on what social media says the filing will show. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Cook’s dissent matters for rate expectations because it widens hawkish support beyond the committee’s usual hard-liners, strengthening the case that a December hike has broad backing. The dissent may also be read politically, given Trump’s efforts to remove her, which adds to scrutiny of Fed independence. Fewer scheduled rate decisions from next year mean each meeting carries more weight, and that could amplify market moves around those dates.

---

Earlier:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 28 Oct: Fed holds rates, yield curve steepens as Big Tech earnings diverge

---

The Fed paused, but with two votes for a hike and a chair insisting the job isn’t done, the pause looks more like a breather than a turn.

Summary:

  • The Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, following last month’s hike
  • Governor Lisa Cook unexpectedly dissented in favour of a hike, her first break from the consensus in more than four years
  • Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also dissented for tighter policy, as she did in April and July
  • Chair Warsh said returning inflation to 2% is paramount and did little to challenge expectations of a December hike
  • The Fed will vote on rates at seven meetings next year and six in 2028, devoting the remaining sessions to strategy
  • The change revises a 45-year-old schedule and fits Warsh’s preference for a quieter Fed

The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate at a range of 3.75% to 4%, pausing after last month’s increase, while leaving markets firmly expecting another hike in December, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The decision itself was widely anticipated. The surprise lay in the dissents. Fed Governor Lisa Cook voted against the hold in favour of a higher rate, breaking with a record of consistently voting with the committee’s consensus since she joined the central bank more than four years ago. Cook, whom President Donald Trump has been trying to remove from her post for more than a year, had recently expressed concern that inflation remains a problem, but had not indicated she saw an urgent need for a further increase.

The second dissent, from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, was more in line with expectations. Hammack has been among the committee’s most hawkish members this year and also dissented in favour of tighter policy in April and July.

At his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Warsh sought to make clear that pausing did not mean the Fed was easing off its effort to bring inflation down. He said returning inflation fully to the 2% target was the overriding priority, that the Fed had recommitted to that goal since he took over, and that last month’s hike marked the start of action. Warsh acknowledged the Fed had not yet achieved price stability but said it was working toward it, and he offered little to challenge the market view that a December increase is coming.

Warsh also announced a change to the Fed’s meeting schedule. Next year, policymakers will vote on rates at only seven of their eight meetings, using the remaining session for a broader strategy discussion. In 2028, that will drop to six rate decisions, with two meetings set aside for strategy. The shift overhauls a calendar that has been in place for 45 years. Warsh first raised the idea internally over the summer.

The move fits his preference for a lower-profile Fed. The post-meeting statement has become shorter under his leadership, and he has opted out of the quarterly dot plot of officials’ projections.

With two officials already pushing for a hike, the December meeting now looms as the next key test of the Fed’s tightening path. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US bitcoin reserve buying 'very soon'? What has to happen first
item.description:
What was said

A Bitcoin Archive post on X this week ran under the banner "$200K+ BITCOIN INCOMING", relaying a claim that U.S. Senator Bill Hagerty says the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve may start buying BTC "very soon" once crypto market rules are settled.

The short answer: the US government has no authority to buy bitcoin on the open market today, the market rules in question stalled in the Senate in September, and "very soon" has been the reserve's estimated time of arrival for the better part of 18 months.

Bitcoin traded around $81,000 on Wednesday, roughly 28% below its level a year earlier. Getting to $200,000 would take a gain of about 2.5 times. That is a lot of weight to hang on one conditional sentence relayed by a social media account.

What the reserve actually is today

President Trump created the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve by executive order on March 6, 2025. It is stocked with bitcoin the government already owns, mostly coins forfeited in criminal and civil cases such as the Silk Road takedown and the Bitfinex hack recovery.

Estimates of the holdings vary by tracker, from about 198,000 BTC to roughly 328,000 BTC. At current prices the upper estimate is worth around $26 billion.

Two rules matter for traders. The order bars the Treasury from selling reserve coins. Any new additions must be budget neutral, so no taxpayer money can be spent buying bitcoin on the open market.

In other words, the reserve is a vault with a lock on the exit and no cash at the entrance.

Why the market rules condition misses the point

The market rules in question are most likely the CLARITY Act, the crypto market structure bill Hagerty has pushed hard all year. It passed the House in July 2025 and cleared the Senate Banking Committee 15 to 9 in May 2026. On September 15 it failed a procedural cloture vote 49 to 50, eleven short of the 60 needed to open debate, after Democrats said their ethics demands over crypto profits made by the president's family had not been met.

Even if CLARITY passed tomorrow, it would not give the Treasury a budget to buy bitcoin. CLARITY decides which regulator oversees which crypto assets. Authority to buy would have to come from separate reserve legislation.

The main House vehicle is the American Reserve Modernization Act (H.R. 8957), introduced in May by Representative Nick Begich with Democrat Jared Golden as co-sponsor. It would lock reserve coins away for at least 20 years and require quarterly proof-of-reserve reports. It does not provide for open-market purchases with appropriated funds. Instead it asks the Treasury to study budget-neutral options, such as revaluing the Federal Reserve's gold certificates at market prices.

So the condition attached to "very soon" is both stalled and, for buying purposes, the wrong one.

A short history of "very soon"

Anyone who has followed this story will recognise the pattern. Newest first:

In fairness, none of these statements has been proven false. The reserve may yet buy bitcoin very soon. It is just that "soon" in Washington appears to run on a different clock from "soon" on crypto X, and the most recent official word put any buying behind an inventory check.

The calendar is not helping either. US midterm elections fall on November 3, and contested crypto legislation rarely speeds up in an election season.

Holding is not buying

This distinction is the lesson worth keeping. Before the 2025 order, US authorities regularly sold forfeited bitcoin, adding supply to the market. The no-sale rule ends that for reserve coins, which removes a potential source of selling pressure. That is a real, if modest, positive.

Not selling is still different from buying. Only an active purchase programme would add new demand, and that needs either a budget-neutral funding method nobody has yet unveiled or a new law from Congress. Bitget chief executive Gracy Chen said in August she does not expect US open-market buying for at least the next two years.

The "$200K incoming" framing skips that step entirely. It treats a conditional remark about a possible future programme as if the purchase orders were already sitting in the queue.

What to watch next

  • CLARITY after the midterms. A fresh cloture attempt in the post-election session would improve the regulatory backdrop, but would not by itself fund any purchases.
  • ARMA's progress. Watch whether H.R. 8957 clears the House Financial Services Committee and reaches a floor vote, and whether a Senate companion gains traction.
  • The promised White House announcement. The test is whether it names a funding source, an amount and a timeline. Custody and accounting updates alone would not mean buying.

What would change the view: a confirmed purchase mechanism with a real source of money behind it. Until then, treat "very soon" as a statement of intent, not a flow of demand.

The practical takeaway: when a headline promises government bitcoin buying, ask two questions. Who has the legal authority to buy, and where does the money come from? If the answer to both is "not yet", so is the $200K. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: Oracle jumps around 11% on $225bn 2030 revenue goal and $20bn cap on new funding

The rally suggests investors had been pricing in more financing risk than profitability risk, so a hard ceiling on new funding did as much work as the revenue target. A capped equity component also limits dilution concerns that had weighed on the stock. Beyond Oracle, a credible path to self-funded AI capacity eases pressure on the broader argument that hyperscaler spending cannot pay for itself. It arrived the same evening as Microsoft and Alphabet reported lower than expected capex. The scale of the move also leaves the stock more sensitive to any slippage against those targets.

---

Oracle gave investors a big number and, more importantly, a spending limit, and the market rewarded the discipline more than the ambition.

Summary:

  • Oracle shares rose around 11% after its Investor Day; no quarterly results were released
  • Fiscal 2030 targets: revenue of $225 billion or more, a non-GAAP operating margin of 40% or higher, and non-GAAP EPS of $21 or more
  • Fiscal 2027 guidance was reaffirmed at revenue of at least $90 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $8.10

  • Capex will peak in fiscal 2027 and 2028, and free cash flow is expected to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028
  • Free cash flow of at least $30 billion is targeted in fiscal 2029, with net debt below 3.5 times adjusted EBITDA

Oracle shares rose around 11% on Wednesday after the company used its Investor Day to set out ambitious long-term growth targets and, just as importantly for investors, put clear limits on how much new money it will raise to fund its AI cloud expansion.

The headline target is revenue of $225 billion or more in fiscal 2030, which implies compound annual growth of more than 35% from fiscal 2026. Oracle also projected a non-GAAP operating margin of at least 40% and non-GAAP earnings per share of $21 or more by that year. For the nearer term, the company reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 guidance for revenue of at least $90 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $8.10.

The event was not an earnings release, and no new quarterly results were reported. The share move instead reflected a reset in how investors view the risk around Oracle’s heavy spending on data centre capacity.

That spending has raised concerns over the company’s debt load, and the funding plan was aimed squarely at those worries. Oracle said new capital-market funding from fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2030 will be capped at $20 billion, excluding refinancing of existing debt, split roughly evenly between equity and gross debt. That comes on top of a $20 billion at-the-market equity raise completed in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The company is also targeting net debt below 3.5 times adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2029.

On cash flow, Oracle expects capital expenditure to peak in fiscal 2027 and 2028 before declining. It forecast free cash flow turning positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reaching at least $30 billion in fiscal 2029, a figure Bloomberg reported was above market estimates. From fiscal 2029, the company expects its growth to be self-funded.

The targets are long-dated and depend on sustained demand for AI computing capacity and on Oracle delivering that capacity on schedule. The fiscal 2028 turn to positive free cash flow will be the first major checkpoint for whether the plan is on track.

item.title: UBS sees limited gold downside as three demand pillars set a floor near $4,000
item.description:
UBS’s view makes $4,000 an ounce (or just below) the level to watch: a sustained break below it would challenge the bank’s dip-buyer floor thesis. Last week’s ETF outflows show that shorter-term investment money has been leaving even as official sector demand holds up. That split suggests near-term price direction may depend on whether central banks and Chinese buyers absorb that selling. For traders, the call frames dips toward $4,000 as areas where buying interest may appear, not as confirmation of a broader downtrend.

----

Fund money may be heading for the exit, but UBS is betting that central banks, Chinese buyers and debt worries will keep gold anchored near $4,000.

Summary:

  • UBS sees gold as a strategic portfolio diversifier, backed by structural demand
  • Gold ETFs recorded net outflows last week, but the bank says long-term fundamentals remain solid
  • Central bank purchases remain strong and Chinese buying is robust
  • Concerns about rising public debt and debt-servicing costs continue to support demand
  • UBS expects structural dip buyers to establish a floor around $4,000 an ounce, limiting downside
  • The bank maintains that further pullbacks are opportunities to add exposure

UBS continues to see gold as a strategic diversifier for portfolios, arguing that structural demand should support higher prices and that the downside from current levels around $4,000 an ounce is limited.

The bank acknowledged that gold exchange-traded funds saw net outflows last week, a sign that some investment demand has eased in the short term. However, UBS said the longer-term fundamentals for bullion remain solid, and it does not view the recent softness in fund flows as a change in the underlying picture.

UBS pointed to three main pillars of support. Central bank buying remains strong, continuing a trend in which official sector institutions have added gold to their reserves. Chinese demand is also robust. The third factor is fiscal: concerns over rising public debt and the growing cost of servicing that debt have not eased, keeping alive one of the longer-running arguments for holding an asset that carries no credit risk.

Taken together, those sources of demand form the basis of UBS’s view that structural dip buyers are likely establishing a floor near the $4,000 level. In practical terms, the bank expects buyers with long investment horizons, such as central banks, to step in on weakness, limiting how far prices can fall.

On that basis, UBS maintains its stance that further pullbacks offer opportunities to add exposure rather than signals to exit.

The view is a recap of the bank’s existing position rather than a new call. It also rests on the assumption that official sector and Chinese buying will continue at a similar pace. A sustained slowdown in either source, or a prolonged run of ETF outflows, would test how firm that $4,000 floor proves to be. For now, UBS’s message to investors is that short-term weakness in flows has not altered its constructive longer-term outlook for gold.

The curve steepened as the front end found some relief from Warsh’s willingness to wait, while longer maturities remained under pressure.

That distinction matters. Less urgency for another near-term hike does not automatically translate into lower borrowing costs across the economy. With the 10-year yield above 5% and oil above $100, longer-term rates continued to present a challenge for housing, business financing and equity valuations.

U.S. stocks: Modest gains, with Nasdaq 100 leading

The Nasdaq 100 led, followed by the Russell 2000. Stocks absorbed both the Fed’s continued inflation concerns and the rise in longer-term yields without a broad retreat.

Major corporate news: Microsoft beats; Alphabet’s cloud strength offsets only part of the weakness

After the close, Microsoft and Alphabet released their recent earnings. 

Microsoft’s fiscal Q1 report exceeded the supplied expectations:

Microsoft also reported cloud revenue of $63.9 billion. Azure’s growth provided an encouraging signal for cloud demand and the monetization of AI-related services.

Alphabet’s Q3 results were more uneven:

  • EPS: $2.12 versus $3.03 expected.
  • Revenue: $127.6 billion versus $127.91 billion expected.
  • Operating income: $40.58 billion versus $43.16 billion expected.

Cloud was Alphabet’s clear bright spot, but the broader revenue and operating-income misses left a more cautious message. The reports gave investors contrasting results to assess heading into the next session. Confirmed after-hours stock reactions were not supplied.

European stocks: Germany gains; Spain and Italy lag

Germany led the supplied major benchmarks, while Spain was the clear underperformer. The uneven finish showed that Europe had little shared direction ahead of the Fed announcement and U.S. technology earnings.

Fed: Inflation target unchanged, December decision open

Warsh reinforced the 2% PCE inflation objective, making clear that there is no softer target. Near-term inflation expectations have risen, but longer-term expectations remain consistent with confidence in the Fed’s ability to restore price stability.

His economic assessment was constructive. Growth has strengthened, employment conditions remain healthy, and business investment is broadening. He also emphasized that improving productivity could allow stronger growth without an equivalent increase in inflation pressure.

The press conference left the Fed in a hold-and-assess position. Warsh declined to prejudge December and described the coming period as information rich. Another hike remains possible, but there was no commitment to deliver one and little indication of urgency to cut. investinglive.com

Crude oil and the Middle East: Diplomatic hopes meet unresolved risks

U.S. crude traded at $101.49, up $1.28 or 1.28%, in the supplied end-of-day snapshot.

Late headlines offered some encouragement on diplomacy. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President Vance had contacted an Iranian hard-liner in an effort to restart peace talks.

NewsNation separately reported substantial exchanges between Iran and the U.S. through mediators over a seven-day proposal intended to prevent a return to military operations after the U.S. midterm elections. Its source described discussions as positive but stressed that nothing had been finalized.

The reporting also remained contradictory. NewsNation’s source disputed earlier reports that the U.S. had informed Gulf allies about a short, intense military campaign after the elections. Traders were therefore left weighing diplomatic progress against the continuing risk of renewed strikes.

On inventories, the weekly EIA report showed crude stocks falling by 1.892 million barrels versus a small build expected. Distillates also declined, but a surprise 3.870-million-barrel gasoline build tempered the otherwise supportive inventory figures. investinglive.com

Oil’s continued elevation keeps the inflation implications of the conflict firmly in focus.

Gold and silver: Gold advances despite higher long yields

Gold traded near $4,077.99, up $17.66 or 0.43%. Silver stood at $54.4436, up $0.0380 or 0.07%.

Gold’s advance came despite the rise in longer-term Treasury yields, which would normally create a headwind. The dollar’s post-Fed retreat and the decline in the 2-year yield offered a supportive counterweight. The mixed full-day dollar performance, however, makes it difficult to attribute the gain to one factor.

Silver posted only a marginal advance, showing less enthusiasm than gold.

Bitcoin: Higher alongside equities

Bitcoin traded at $81,608, up $797 or 0.99%.

Its advance was consistent with the positive tone in equities. No separate crypto-specific catalyst was established in the available material.

The overall takeaway

The Fed is willing to wait, but inflation remains the constraint. The next session starts with longer-term Treasury yields still elevated, contrasting Microsoft and Alphabet earnings to digest, and Middle East negotiations that have yet to deliver an agreement. Oil remains a key link between the geopolitical headlines and the interest-rate outlook.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Vance writes to Iran hard-liner Rezaei to revive talks as Trump weighs new strikes
item.description:
For oil, the report adds a two-way risk ahead of next week’s midterms. A credible negotiating channel offers the first sign in months that Hormuz shipping could eventually be unlocked, which would ease the supply premium. But the contacts cover only a framework, and Trump continues to signal strikes. That leaves the market exposed to a sharp upside move if talks fail and an attack follows. Rezaei’s recent threats against the UAE add another layer of Gulf supply risk, so traders are likely to keep paying for protection until there is clarity on Trump’s decision.

---

Washington is talking to Tehran’s hard-liners in private while threatening war in public, and the oil market has to price both.

Summary:

  • Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, reportedly at Trump’s direction
  • The aim is to find enough common ground to dissuade Trump from ordering a short, intense strike in the coming weeks
  • Contacts have focused on a negotiating framework, not specific peace terms, and Rezaei says core demands must be met first
  • Trump has publicly denied negotiating and says he expects a return to war after the midterms
  • A June memorandum of understanding collapsed over Strait of Hormuz shipping, and talks via Qatar and Pakistan remain deadlocked
  • The US blockade of Iranian ports continues, and oil flows through Hormuz have not been enough to ease high energy prices

US Vice President JD Vance has written to one of Iran’s most powerful hard-liners in an attempt to revive stalled peace talks, even as President Donald Trump signals that a return to war could follow next week’s midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.

According to the report, Vance sent the letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and formerly the longest-serving commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. One person said the letter was sent at Trump’s direction, and the president is aware of the outreach. The aim is to test whether enough common ground exists to dissuade Trump from ordering a short, intense strike on Iran in the coming weeks.

The contacts so far have reportedly focused on a possible framework for negotiations rather than the details of a peace proposal. Rezaei said last week that Tehran would not negotiate until certain core demands were met. Some US officials believe engaging the hard-liners, who have gained influence since US and Israeli strikes killed regime leaders at the start of the war, could produce a better diplomatic outcome.

The outreach sits awkwardly with Trump’s public stance. Last week he said Washington was not negotiating with Iran and suggested strikes were coming soon, and on the campaign trail he has said he expects a return to war. On Tuesday he accused Tehran of stalling, possibly in hope of an election result that he said would not help it.

Diplomacy has repeatedly broken down. A memorandum of understanding agreed in June fell apart within two weeks over differing interpretations of how to reopen shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Talks through mediators Qatar and Pakistan remain deadlocked, with Washington seeking upfront nuclear concessions and Tehran demanding immediate economic relief. A US blockade of Iranian ports remains in place, and while some oil continues to move through the strait, flows have not been enough to ease high energy prices.

Rezaei has taken a hawkish line, warning earlier this month that Iran could target the United Arab Emirates as well as data centres and internet cables across the region. On Sunday, however, he met security chiefs from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey in Tehran as all sides sought de-escalation. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran remained ready to defend itself but was still giving diplomacy a chance.

The political stakes are high in Washington too. Republicans are bracing for losses in Congress, with voters citing the war and rising fuel costs, and Vance is the early front-runner for the party’s 2028 presidential nomination. Whether this channel can produce a framework before Trump makes a final decision on strikes is now the key question for both the conflict and energy markets. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Alphabet Q3: Google Cloud revenue jumps 103% but search and ad sales miss forecasts
item.description:
The quarter sets Cloud strength against core advertising weakness, and the search miss is likely to dominate the initial reaction. Search remains the profit engine funding Alphabet’s AI build-out. Capex came in about $4.4 billion below forecast, after Microsoft also underspent earlier in the evening, so traders may question the near-term pace of hyperscaler orders for AI chips and data centre equipment. The equity securities loss inflates the headline EPS decline, so expect focus on underlying operating performance, where the miss is smaller but still present.

---

Earlier:

  • Microsoft Q1 beats as Azure grows 48% and capex lands $6bn below forecast

---

Google Cloud doubled and beat, but the advertising businesses that pay for Alphabet’s AI ambitions came up short, leaving investors weighing tomorrow’s growth against today’s profit engine.

Summary:

  • EPS of $2.12, down from $2.87 a year earlier, weighed by a net loss of around $8.7 billion on equity securities
  • Revenue of around $127.6 billion narrowly missed estimates of about $127.9 billion
  • Google Cloud revenue grew 103% to around $31 billion, beating forecasts of about $29 billion
  • Search and other revenue of around $63 billion and YouTube ads of around $11.2 billion both missed expectations
  • Operating income of around $41 billion missed forecasts of about $43 billion
  • Capex of around $51 billion came in below the roughly $56 billion expected
  • YouTube Music and Premium subscriptions passed 150 million, and the company says its Gemini 4 models lead at the frontier

Alphabet’s third-quarter results delivered a split verdict, with Google Cloud more than doubling its revenue and beating forecasts while the core advertising businesses fell short of expectations and an investment loss dragged down earnings.

Earnings per share came in at $2.12, down from $2.87 a year earlier, a decline of about 26%. A large part of that drop traces to a net loss of around $8.7 billion on equity securities, a non-operating item tied to the value of Alphabet’s investment holdings rather than the performance of its businesses. Total revenue of around $127.6 billion was marginally below the roughly $127.9 billion analysts had expected.

Google Cloud was the clear bright spot. Revenue grew 103% to around $31 billion, well ahead of forecasts of about $29 billion, confirming strong demand for the AI computing capacity and services that hyperscalers are racing to supply.

The picture was weaker in the businesses that still generate most of Alphabet’s revenue. Google Services revenue reached around $96 billion, short of the roughly $98 billion expected. Within that, Search and other revenue came in at around $63 billion against estimates of about $65 billion, and YouTube advertising revenue of around $11.2 billion missed forecasts of about $11.4 billion. Search is the segment watched most closely for signs that AI-driven answers are eroding traditional query advertising, so a shortfall of around $1.5 billion is likely to revive that debate, even if the quarter alone cannot prove a trend.

Operating income of around $41 billion also missed the consensus of about $43 billion. Capital expenditure totalled around $51 billion, below the roughly $56 billion analysts had forecast.

The company said its Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon models now lead at the frontier of AI performance, and that YouTube Music and Premium have passed 150 million subscribers globally, a growing source of non-advertising revenue.

The earnings call will be key for guidance on capex, the search outlook and whether Cloud’s growth can keep offsetting softness in advertising. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Microsoft Q1 beats as Azure grows 48% and capex lands $6bn below forecast
item.description:
The capex figure is likely to drive the reaction as much as the beat itself. Lower than expected spending alongside stronger Azure growth supports Microsoft’s margins and its AI return-on-investment case. It could weigh on sentiment toward AI hardware and data centre suppliers if traders read it as a slowdown in hyperscaler orders. The result also sets a high bar for the AI cloud trade into the remaining megacap reports.

---

Microsoft grew Azure faster than expected on far less capital spending than forecast, a combination that strengthens its AI payback story but will raise questions about the pace of the build-out.

Summary:

  • Adjusted EPS of $4.89 beat the $4.73 consensus; reported EPS was $4.92
  • Revenue of around $92 billion topped estimates of about $91 billion
  • Operating income of around $46 billion beat forecasts of about $44 billion
  • Cloud revenue reached around $64 billion, ahead of the roughly $62 billion expected
  • Azure revenue grew 48% excluding currency effects, versus forecasts of about 45%
  • Capital expenditure of around $39 billion fell well short of the roughly $46 billion analysts had projected

Microsoft beat Wall Street expectations across its main metrics in its fiscal first quarter, with Azure growth accelerating well past forecasts while capital spending came in sharply below what analysts had pencilled in.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at $4.89, ahead of the $4.73 consensus, while reported EPS was $4.92. Revenue reached around $92 billion, roughly $1.7 billion above the estimate of about $91 billion. Operating income of around $46 billion topped expectations by roughly $2 billion, pointing to solid margins alongside the revenue beat.

The cloud business remained the centrepiece. Cloud revenue climbed to around $64 billion, against forecasts of about $62 billion, and Azure revenue grew 48% excluding currency effects, comfortably above the roughly 45% analysts had expected. Azure growth is the figure investors watch most closely as a gauge of corporate demand for AI services running on Microsoft’s infrastructure, so a beat of more than three percentage points is a meaningful outperformance.

The surprise in the release was capital expenditure. Microsoft spent around $39 billion in the quarter, well short of the roughly $46 billion analysts had projected, a gap of more than $6 billion. That contrast will draw attention. Delivering faster Azure growth on lower than expected spending suggests the company is extracting more revenue from capacity already built, which supports the return-on-investment case for its AI build-out.

The lower capex figure can be read more than one way, however. It may reflect the timing of equipment deliveries, data centre construction schedules or supply constraints rather than a deliberate slowdown, and the quarterly number alone does not show which. Management’s commentary on the earnings call, and any update to full-year spending plans, will be needed to judge whether the shortfall is a one-quarter timing effect or a change in the investment trajectory.

The call and the company’s guidance for the current quarter, particularly for Azure growth and capital spending, will now set the tone for the stock in the next session. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
